stances.claim: Top executive and legislative officials are 'unleashing their superpowers' to bring Rep. Arnolfo Teves Jr. to justice for the brutal killing of Gov. Roel Degamo - through six separate prongs.

First, the 292-member House led by Speaker Romualdez unanimously suspended Teves for 60 days for 'defying orders' to return in person - and per Alejandrino v. Quezon (Sept 11, 1924), the Constitution caps representative suspension at 60 days to avoid a hiatus, 'without ruling out expulsion that may lead to a special election' (Romualdez's warning of more 'disciplinary actions' may signal expulsion intent).
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-historical anchor (98-year-old case as the constitutional ceiling)

stances.claim: Second, Remulla wants Teves tagged as 'terrorist' via Anti-Terrorism Council/CA to extricate him from Cambodia (no PH-Cambodia extradition treaty), so UN-member states would be obligated under international law to arrest and return him. But the Puno-chaired committee drafting terrorism-case rules has not finished; per Puno even ex-parte proceedings must actively protect respondent constitutional rights.

While CJ agrees the full might of the state should be used to attain justice, 'I believe laws should not be weaponized' - the Anti-Terrorism Act should not be resorted to merely to bring Teves in. The law should be used only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction shown by the evidence at hand'; 'his return is merely the consequence, not the reason, for prosecuting him under that law. I am not for or against Teves. I am for the rule of law.'
Third, with DFA help, Remulla convinced Timor-Leste (where Teves flew from Cambodia) to deny asylum - though Teves may ask for reconsideration.
Fourth, an Interpol 'Notice' has been issued obligating foreign police forces to report Teves's presence - enabling Philippine police tracking.

Fifth, Remulla will ask DFA to cancel Teves's passport - but the right to travel is constitutionally guaranteed, and by law a passport may be cancelled only when the holder (a) is a fugitive, (b) is convicted of a crime, (c) acquired the passport fraudulently, or (d) requests cancellation due to loss/tampering. 'At this point, none of these four causes exists.'

Sixth, murder charges will be filed shortly - Remulla expects this will support declaring Teves a 'fugitive' enabling DFA passport cancellation. But Remulla himself directed prosecutors to file only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction' (per CJ's Feb 20 column 'Don't charge what you can't prove'); 'IMHO' that directive should apply to Teves's high-profile case despite originally covering first-level courts.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-binding-directive critique plus cross-reference to own prior column

notable_anecdotes: The 99-year-old Alejandrino v. Quezon (September 11, 1924) constitutional anchor for the 60-day suspension ceiling - making this column a useful historical-doctrinal reference for House discipline limits.

CJ's signature principled-neutrality declaration - 'I am not for or against Teves. I am for the rule of law' - one of his cleanest single-line articulations of the rule-of-law-over-personality stance, deployed in a high-temperature murder-mastermind case.

The 'laws should not be weaponized' principle - explicitly applied to the Anti-Terrorism Act, with the operative test 'reasonable certainty of conviction shown by the evidence at hand' rather than mere instrumental utility.
The 'his return is merely the consequence, not the reason' framing - CJ's most precise single-line articulation of the means-ends test for prosecuting under specialized criminal statutes.

The four-ground statutory passport-cancellation enumeration followed by 'At this point, none of these four causes exists' - a clean statutory-fit analysis showing the gap between desired action and existing legal authority.

CJ's deployment of Remulla's own February 20 directive AGAINST Remulla - using the secretary's own 'reasonable certainty of conviction' standard to caution against the imminent murder filing being driven by passport-cancellation logic.

The CJ Puno terrorism-rules-committee detail - preserving the institutional readiness gap (rules drafted but not yet SC-approved; ex-parte proceedings allowed but constitutional rights actively protected).
Ferdinand Topacio named as lead Teves counsel - preserving the death-threats-as-defense framing.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the six-prong executive-and-legislative effort 'unleashing their superpowers' to bring Negros Oriental Rep. Arnolfo Teves Jr. to justice for the brutal killing of Gov. Roel Degamo of the same province - denounced by Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla as an alleged mastermind. First, the 292-member House led by Speaker Martin Romualdez unanimously suspended Teves (still abroad) for 60 days for 'defying orders' to return in person; per Alejandrino v. Quezon (September 11, 1924), the Constitution caps representative suspension at 60 days to avoid a hiatus in district representation, 'without ruling out expulsion that may lead to a special election' - Romualdez's warning of more 'disciplinary actions' may signal expulsion. His lawyers led by Ferdinand Topacio claim Teves is willing to come home except for 'serious and credible death threats,' despite President Marcos's safety assurances. Second, Remulla wants Teves tagged as 'terrorist' via the Anti-Terrorism Council and/or Court of Appeals to extricate him from Cambodia (no PH-Cambodia extradition treaty exists), so any UN-member state where Teves is found would be obligated under international law to arrest and return him. But the committee drafting terrorism-case rules headed by retired CJ Reynato S. Puno has not finished its work - and per CJ Puno, even ex-parte proceedings must actively protect respondent constitutional rights. While Panganiban agrees the full might of the state should be used to attain justice, 'I believe laws should not be weaponized' - the Anti-Terrorism Act should not be resorted to merely to bring Teves in; the law should be used only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction shown by the evidence at hand.' 'His return is merely the consequence, not the reason, for prosecuting him under that law. I am not for or against Teves. I am for the rule of law.' Third, with DFA help, Remulla convinced Timor-Leste (where Teves flew from Cambodia) to deny his asylum application - though Teves may ask for reconsideration. Fourth, an Interpol 'Notice' has been issued obligating foreign police forces to report Teves's presence in their jurisdictions, enabling Philippine police tracking. Fifth, Remulla will ask the DFA to cancel Teves's passport - but the right to travel is constitutionally guaranteed, and by law a passport may be cancelled only when the holder (a) is a fugitive, (b) is convicted of a crime, (c) acquired the passport fraudulently, or (d) requests cancellation due to loss or tampering - 'at this point, none of these four causes exists.' Sixth, murder charges against Teves will be filed shortly, and Remulla expects the filing will support declaring Teves a 'fugitive' enabling DFA passport cancellation - but Remulla himself directed prosecutors to file criminal cases only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction' (per CJ's February 20 column 'Don't charge what you can't prove'), and although that directive originally covered first-level courts, 'IMHO' it should apply to Teves's high-profile case and others as well.
